newsitem.title: USA: US pasta group urges free wheat flow from Canada.
newsitem.headline: US pasta group urges free wheat flow from Canada.

text.p: U.S. pasta producers are urging the Clinton administration not to block wheat imports coming from Canada, despite pressure from Northern state Democrats to take that action.
"We're concerned about supply availability," Jula Kinniard, president of the National Pasta Association told Reuters.
With the U.S. durum wheat crop forecast to drop 30 percent this year, "we're really going to need imports to help make up the shortfall," she said.
Durum is the key ingredient in pasta.

On Thursday, U.S. Agriculture Secretary and U.S. Trade Ambassador Charlene Barshefsky will meet with Senators Kent Conrad and Byron Dorgan, both North Dakota Democrats, and Senator Tim Johnson, a South Dakota Democrat, to discuss the issue.

Last week, Dorgan urged Barshefsky and Glickman to "shut down" wheat imports from Canada and use the Export Enhancement Program to subsidize U.S. wheat sales to other countries now buying Canadian wheat and durum.
Such action would "send a strong signal to Canada that it will pay a significant price for pouring its wheat into the U.S.," Dorgan said.
In 1994, U.S. wheat producer concern over a dramatic surge in imports from Canada prompted the Clinton administration to impose a one-year, 1.5-million-tonne limit.
After that expired, the Clinton administration said it would continue to monitor shipments from Canada using the former quota level as reference point for deciding whether to take further action.

On Tuesday, USDA Chief Economist Keith Collins told reporters that he did know of any trade policy tool--other than negotiation--that the United States could use to restrict wheat imports from Canada. The U.S. gave up the authority
it used to impose the 1994/95 import quota when it signed the Uruguay Round trade agreement. So, Canada would have to agree to any restrictions, Collins said.

During the 1996/97 U.S. wheat marketing year that ended May 31, U.S. wheat imports from Canada totaled about 2.0 million tonnes, up sharply from the previous year and the third highest level on record.

A number of factors contributed to the increase including tight U.S. wheat supplies and congestion at western Canadian export ports that pushed wheat down into the U.S. instead, said Ed Allen, an international wheat trade analyst in USDA's Economic Research Service.
In addition, wheat imports from Canada could rise even higher in 1997/98 depending on the final size of the U.S. spring harvest and whether Canada is able to resolve its port difficulties, he said.

Earlier this month, USDA forecast the 1997/98 U.S. hard red spring wheat crop at 513 million bushels, down sharply 627 million in 1996/97. It also pegged the U.S. durum crop at 81 million bushels, down from 116 million last year.

In response to expected small durum harvest, the U.S. pasta industry has launched its own letter writing campaign to President Clinton, Barshefsky and members of Congress urging that no restrictions be put on imports from Canada.
Durum prices--which were already high--have risen since the crop report, resulting in increased input costs for U.S. pasta producers, Kinniard said.
At the same time, the industry continues to face strong import competition from Turkey and especially Italy, despite recent tariffs imposed by the U.S., she said.
